slides.heading: Right Smaller Than
slides.subtitle: AlgoExpert · Very Hard · Binary Search Trees
slides.narration: Let's solve Right Smaller Than, a very hard binary search trees problem. We'll restate the problem, build the intuition, walk through the approach, read the Java solution, and finish with its complexity.

slides.heading: The problem
bullets: For each element, how many elements to its right are strictly smaller?
Insert from the right into an augmented BST tracking left-subtree sizes.
slides.narration: Here's the problem. For each element, how many elements to its right are strictly smaller? Insert from the right into an augmented BST tracking left-subtree sizes.

slides.heading: Intuition
bullets: Insert from the right into a BST that knows its left-subtree sizes; each insert counts the smaller values already there.
slides.narration: Insert from the right into a BST that knows its left-subtree sizes; each insert counts the smaller values already there.

slides.heading: Brute force vs optimal
bullets: For each element, scan right → O(n²)
BST with left-subtree sizes → O(n log n) average
Merge-sort counting or BIT → O(n log n) worst
slides.narration: Scanning right from every element is quadratic. Inserting right to left into a BST that tracks left-subtree sizes counts smaller values during insertion.

slides.heading: Approach
bullets: 3. Add left sizes when going right
slides.narration: Step by step. First, iterate from the end. Second, insert into an augmented BST. Third, add left sizes when going right. Fourth, record the count.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: Insert 2: 0 smaller to its right
slides.narration: Moving right to left, insert 2 into a BST of everything to its right. Every time we go right, we add the left-subtree size plus one: 0 smaller values.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: Insert 3: 1 smaller to its right
slides.narration: Moving right to left, insert 3 into a BST of everything to its right. Every time we go right, we add the left-subtree size plus one: 1 smaller values.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: Insert 11: 4 smaller to its right
slides.narration: Moving right to left, insert 11 into a BST of everything to its right. Every time we go right, we add the left-subtree size plus one: 4 smaller values.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: Insert 8: 5 smaller to its right
slides.narration: Moving right to left, insert 8 into a BST of everything to its right. Every time we go right, we add the left-subtree size plus one: 5 smaller values.

slides.heading: Java solution (1/2)
slides.narration: We insert from the end. Going left increments that node's left size; going right adds left size plus one, unless equal. The accumulated count is the answer for that index.

slides.heading: Java solution (2/2)
slides.narration: We insert from the end. Going left increments that node's left size; going right adds left size plus one, unless equal. The accumulated count is the answer for that index.

slides.heading: Complexity
bullets: Time: O(n log n) avg, O(n^2) worst
slides.narration: Time is O of n log n avg, O of n squared worst. Space is O of n.

slides.heading: Edge cases & pitfalls
slides.narration: A sorted input makes the BST degenerate; a Fenwick tree avoids that.

slides.heading: Interview tips & follow-ups
slides.narration: Mention the Fenwick-tree and merge-sort alternatives.

slides.heading: Recap
bullets: Insert from the right into a BST that knows its left-subtree sizes; each insert counts the smaller values already there.
Complexity: O(n log n) avg, O(n^2) worst
slides.narration: To recap Right Smaller Than: Insert from the right into a BST that knows its left-subtree sizes; each insert counts the smaller values already there. Try re-implementing it from scratch without looking.
